{{Short description|Extinct Uto-Aztecan languages of Mexico}} {{Infobox language | name = Ópata | ethnicity = [[Opata people|Opata]] | region = [[Sonora]], [[Arizona]] | familycolor = Uto-Aztecan | fam1 = [[Uto-Aztecan languages|Uto-Aztecan]] | glotto = opat1247 | glottorefname = Opata–Eudeve | ELP = 4927 | ELPname = Ópata | fam3 = Opatan | extinct = 1930s | ref = e18 | states = [[Mexico]], [[U.S.]] | nativename = {{lang|opt|Teguima}} | altname = | revived = 21st century | dia1 = Teguima/Opata | dia2 = [[Eudeve language|Eudeve]] | imagecaption = Vocabulary of the Opata language of unknown date and origin, part of the collection of the [[Cervantine Library]] in [[Monterrey]] | image = Vocab lengua opata (1).pdf | map = Uto-Aztecan_map.svg | mapcaption = {{legend|a5bbd3|Opatan}} | linglist = opt | linglist2 = 0vv | lingname2 = Jova | lingname = Eudeve | iso3 = opt }} '''Ópata''' (also '''Tegüima,''' '''Teguima, Tehuima, Tehui''', '''Jova, Joval, Tonichi, Sonori''' and '''Ure'''; {{langx|opt|Teguima}}) is either of two closely related [[Uto-Aztecan languages|Uto-Aztecan]] languages, '''''Teguima''''' and ''[[Eudeve language|Eudeve]]'', spoken by the [[Opata people]] of northern central [[Sonora]] in [[Mexico]] and Southeast of Arizona in the United States. It was believed to be dead already in 1930, and [[Carl Sofus Lumholtz]] reported the Opata to have become "Mexicanized" and lost their language and customs already when traveling through Sonora in the 1890s. In a 1993 survey by the [[Instituto Nacional Indigenista]], 15 people in the [[Mexican Federal District]] self-identified as speakers of Ópata.{{cite web| url = http://www.ethnologue.com/show_language.asp?code=opt| title = Opata {{!}} Ethnologue}} This may not mean, however, that the language was actually living, since linguistic nomenclature in Mexico is notoriously fuzzy. Sometimes Eudeve is called Opata, a term which should be restricted to Teguima. ''Eudeve'' (which is split into the ''Heve'' (''Egue'') and ''Dohema'' dialects) and ''Teguima'' (also called ''Ópata'', ''Ore'') are distinct languages, but sometimes have been considered merely dialects of one single language. The [[INALI]] (Mexican National Institute for Indigenous Languages) does not count Opata among the currently extant indigenous languages of Mexico.[http://site.inali.gob.mx/pdf/libro_lenguas_indigenas_nacionales_en_riesgo_de_desaparicion.pdf INALI] == Classification == Opata had long been considered to be part of the [[Taracahitic languages]], but this is no longer considered a valid genetic unit.Shaul, D. Vol. 8, No. 2 == Revival == Although the Opata Nation, an [[unrecognized tribe]], considers the language inactive, they are in the process of its language revitalization.{{Cite web |date=2019-05-20 |title=Language - Official Opata Nation website |url=https://opatanation.org/language |access-date=2025-01-20 |language=en-US}} The Fundación OPATA-TEGUIMA launched the first-ever Opata Living Dictionary in 2021 in collaboration with Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages. ==Phonology== === Consonants === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" ! colspan="2" rowspan="2" | ! rowspan="2" |[[Labial consonant|Labial]] ! rowspan="2" |[[Dental consonant|Dental]] ! rowspan="2" |[[Alveolar consonant|Alveolar]] ! rowspan="2" |[[Palatal consonant|Palatal]] ! colspan="2" |[[Velar consonant|Velar]] ! rowspan="2" |[[Glottal consonant|Glottal]] |- !plain ![[Labialization|lab.]] |- ! colspan="2" |[[Nasal consonant|Nasal]] |{{IPA link|m}} | |{{IPA link|n}} | | | | |- ! rowspan="2" |[[Plosive]]/
